chapter_title: Cloning and Exploring the Hyperledger Fabric Samples Repository
chapter_summary:
With our development environment prerequisites in place, we're now ready to acquire the official Hyperledger Fabric samples. The `fabric-samples` repository is an indispensable resource provided by the Hyperledger project. It contains a wealth of examples, scripts, and configurations that serve as a starting point for building and experimenting with Fabric networks. For anyone pursuing Hyperledger Fabric certification, understanding this repository is fundamental, as it provides the `test-network` we'll use extensively and reference chaincode implementations.

To begin, we'll use `Git` to clone the `fabric-samples` repository from its official GitHub location. It's crucial to clone a specific release branch that aligns with the Fabric version you intend to work with. While the `main` branch always has the latest code, it might be unstable or incompatible with the stable Fabric binaries you'll download later. For certification purposes, it's best to stick to a stable release branch, for example, `release-2.5` or `release-2.4`, depending on the target Fabric version for the certification.
```bash
# Navigate to your desired development directory
cd ~/development # or C:\Users\YourUser\development
# Clone the fabric-samples repository, specifying a release branch
git clone https://github.com/hyperledger/fabric-samples.git --branch release-2.5
# Navigate into the cloned directory
cd fabric-samples
```
After cloning, take a moment to explore the directory structure. This repository is not just a collection of random files; it's organized logically to provide various examples and utilities. You'll notice several top-level directories, each serving a distinct purpose:

*   `test-network/`: This is arguably the most important directory for our initial setup. It contains a minimal, yet fully functional, Hyperledger Fabric network configuration using Docker Compose. We'll be spending a lot of time here, learning how to bring up, tear down, and interact with a basic Fabric network. It includes scripts to deploy peers, orderers, CAs, and even deploy sample chaincode.
*   `chaincode/`: This directory holds various chaincode examples implemented in different languages (Go, Node.js, Java). You'll find simple asset management chaincode (`asset-transfer-basic`) and more complex scenarios. These examples are invaluable for understanding chaincode structure, API interactions, and best practices.
*   `bin/`: This directory is typically empty after cloning but will be populated with Hyperledger Fabric binaries (like `peer`, `orderer`, `configtxgen`, `cryptogen`) when you run the `bootstrap.sh` script, which we'll cover in the next chapter.
*   `commercial-paper/`: A more advanced example demonstrating a commercial paper use case, showcasing how to model complex business processes on Fabric.
*   `first-network/`: An older, more complex example of a Fabric network setup. While historically significant, the `test-network` has largely superseded it for simplicity and ease of use in recent Fabric versions.
*   `fabcar/`: A classic introductory example that demonstrates a simple car dealership scenario, often used for initial client application development tutorials.
*   `asset-transfer-basic/`: A modern, simpler asset transfer chaincode example, often preferred over `fabcar` for new learners due to its clarity and focus on core chaincode concepts.

Understanding this layout helps you quickly locate relevant files and examples. For instance, if you're looking to start a local network, you'll head to `test-network`. If you need to see how to write chaincode, the `chaincode` directory is your destination. A common mistake is to clone the `main` branch without realizing it might be ahead of the stable Fabric binaries, leading to compatibility issues. Always specify a stable release branch with the `--branch` flag during cloning. This repository is your sandbox for learning and experimentation, so getting familiar with its contents now will greatly accelerate your learning process.

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how to safely acquire the official fabric-samples repository and why it matters for local Hyperledger Fabric development. The fabric-samples collection is the canonical sandbox provided by the project: it includes minimal networks, sample chaincode implementations in multiple languages, and helper scripts you'll rely on during certification labs. We'll emphasize an important practice: clone a specific release branch so the sample scripts match the Fabric binaries you install. Practically, you'll run a git clone command with the --branch flag, then inspect the top-level directories to find test-network and chaincode folders. This knowledge prevents a common pitfall where the main branch moves ahead of stable platform binaries, which leads to mismatched scripts or missing tools. By the end of the chapter you'll be comfortable cloning a release-aligned copy, navigating the main folders, and identifying where network orchestration files and sample smart contracts live. That preparation saves time when you bring up a local network and deploy sample chaincode, and it keeps your environment reproducible for certification exercises. Consider what release you need for your target labs and always verify the branch before cloning.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: We will make four practical skills the focus of this chapter. First, you'll learn how to clone the official fabric-samples repository using Git with a release branch, so your samples match the binaries you install. Second, you will learn how to inspect the repository layout and locate the primary working directories such as test-network and chaincode. Third, you will be able to identify example chaincode implementations and the languages they use so you can choose an appropriate sample to deploy. Fourth, you'll understand the role of the bin directory and the bootstrap script that populates it with Fabric tools. Each objective is tied to a small verification milestone: run the git clone command, list top-level folders, open a sample chaincode folder, and inspect the presence or absence of binaries before running bootstrap. These tasks matter because they make your local lab reproducible and reduce errors when you bring up containers or install binaries. A common misconception is that cloning main is safe; instead, pin a release branch to ensure compatibility. By practicing the four checkpoints you'll be ready to bring up a test network and deploy sample chaincode in subsequent chapters.

screens.title: Cloning the repository with git
screens.subtitle: Use git clone with --branch to get a release-aligned copy of fabric-samples

narration.text: Cloning the fabric-samples repository is the first hands-on step. The key principle is to clone a release branch that matches the Fabric binaries you'll later install. A practical command is git clone https://github. com/hyperledger/fabric-samples. git --branch release-2.5. This command creates a local folder named fabric-samples with the files at that release. After cloning, change into the folder and run a directory listing to confirm expected folders are present. A common misconception is that cloning the main branch is always fine; main may have forward changes that require newer binaries or modified scripts. For certification labs, reproducibility matters more than the latest features, so pin a stable release. Concrete example: if your lab uses Fabric 2.5 binaries, cloning release-2.5 prevents mismatches in network. sh or bootstrap expectations. Try this in your terminal and capture the output. If you see an error about branches or permissions, check your network access or the repository URL. Takeaway: a branch-pinned clone reduces later friction and is a simple reproducible step to prepare your workspace. How will you verify that your clone aligns with your target binaries?

screens.title: What is fabric-samples and why it matters
screens.subtitle: Understand the repository's role as the canonical learning sandbox

narration.text: The fabric-samples repository is the official collection of example networks, chaincode samples, and utility scripts maintained by the Hyperledger community. Define it mentally as a sandbox: a curated set of working examples you can run locally to learn and test platform features. It contains multiple folders each with a specific purpose. For example, test-network is a small, modern network configuration good for rapid labs. Chaincode contains smart contracts written in Go, Node. js and Java, offering real-world patterns for asset transfer or commercial paper. The bin directory is intended to hold platform executables after running the bootstrap script. A misconception learners often have is expecting all necessary executables to appear immediately after clone; instead, bootstrap populates bin and ensures binaries match the release. Concrete example: when you open chaincode/asset-transfer-basic you'll see language-specific folders with README files and source code that illustrate how client applications interact with chaincode APIs. Why it matters: using these examples reduces development time and provides validated patterns to copy, adapt, and test in your certification labs. Which sample will you explore first? screens.title: Inspecting test-network
screens.subtitle: Identify scripts and folders used to start a minimal Fabric network

narration.text: The test-network directory is the immediate place you'll go to bring up a local Fabric environment. It is designed to be minimal but complete: it contains orchestration scripts, an organizations folder for MSP materials, docker compose files, and a network. sh script that sequences creation, deployment, and teardown. When you cd into test-network and run ls, expect to see network. sh, organizations, scripts, and configtx directories. A concrete action is to open network. sh and look for commented steps that show how the script calls binaries like peer and configtxgen; scanning comments gives you a preview of what the script will perform. A common misconception is that test-network automatically runs on clone; it does not. You must have the right binaries in bin and Docker installed to run these scripts. Example: network. sh provides commands to create a channel, deploy chaincode, and bring down the network. Understanding these parts helps you anticipate the runtime dependencies and prepares you to read error messages if something fails. Takeaway: reading test-network files before execution reduces surprises and informs which binaries and Docker images you must have available.

screens.title: Comparing example folders: test-network vs first-network
screens.subtitle: Why test-network is recommended for labs

narration.text: Two notable example network folders in fabric-samples are test-network and first-network. Test-network is modern, minimal, and focused on rapid bring-up using Docker Compose and helper scripts. First-network is older and more complex; it historically illustrated more manual steps and configuration file generation. For hands-on certification labs, test-network is preferred because it reduces setup complexity and includes network. sh which sequences common tasks like channel creation and chaincode deployment. A concrete comparison: test-network contains a single network. sh orchestrator and a tidy organizations folder, whereas first-network includes more verbose templates and historical scripts that are useful for deep learning but can be unnecessarily complex for initial labs. A common misconception is that older examples are always better documentation — in practice, newer simplified examples reduce friction and better match current tooling. If you need advanced configuration patterns, first-network is a reference, but begin with test-network to get a working local environment quickly. Takeaway: start with test-network to learn the essentials, then explore first-network when you want to study legacy patterns or advanced customization. screens.title: Understanding the bin directory and bootstrap script
screens.subtitle: Why bin is empty after clone and how bootstrap populates it

narration.text: After cloning fabric-samples you will commonly find the bin directory present but empty. This is intentional. The repository does not carry large platform binaries in version control. Instead, a bootstrap. sh script downloads or populates the bin folder with platform executables like peer, orderer, configtxgen, and cryptogen that match the specified release. The recommended flow is to review bootstrap. sh, understand which binaries it expects, and run it after you confirm network requirements and Docker availability. A concrete scenario: if you clone release-2.5, run bootstrap. sh with the matching version tags so the downloaded binaries align with test-network scripts. A common mistake is to assume bin contains the executables already; when you run network. sh without populated binaries you will see missing command errors. Always inspect the README and the bootstrap script options to avoid mismatched runtime versions. Takeaway: bootstrap bridges the gap between repository examples and the platform executables required to run them, and you should run it only after confirming the release branch you cloned. screens.title: Common mistakes and quick troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: How to recognize branch, missing binaries, and Docker issues

narration.text: As you clone and explore, a few recurring issues commonly trip learners. First, cloning main instead of a release often produces errors because the sample scripts assume newer or different binaries. The quick check is to run git branch --show-current inside the cloned folder and confirm it matches your intended release. Second, missing binaries in bin produce "command not found" errors when scripts call peer or configtxgen; verify bin contents before running network. sh and run bootstrap. sh if necessary. Third, Docker or Docker Compose not running will cause container creation failures; ensure Docker is installed and the daemon is active. Fourth, permission errors can occur on Windows or when filesystem paths contain spaces; prefer a development path with no spaces. For each issue, the remedy is straightforward: confirm branch, populate bin, start Docker, and use a clean path. A misconception is assuming errors mean the sample is broken. More often they indicate a local environment mismatch. Takeaway: systematic checks of branch, bin, Docker, and path reduce time lost to troubleshooting. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three essential concepts you should carry forward. First, always clone a release branch of fabric-samples to keep samples and binaries compatible; this prevents many avoidable errors. Second, test-network is the recommended, minimal entrypoint for labs — read network. sh and supporting readmes before running scripts. Third, chaincode examples and the bin directory are your working resources: pick a chaincode that matches your preferred language and run bootstrap to populate bin before attempting network orchestration. These concise ideas form the practical habits that will make your local Fabric labs reliable and reproducible.
